whyThisMatters: A lot of what feels obviously true about cybersecurity is outdated advice or half-right — a few minutes here clears up the ones that actually matter.
rememberThis: If a security "rule" sounds like something from 10 years ago, it's worth double-checking before you follow it.

items.myth: You can always tell a phishing email because of bad spelling and grammar.
items.fact: Modern phishing emails are often polished and professional — many are written or cleaned up with AI tools now, so spelling mistakes are no longer a reliable warning sign.
items.detail: The real tell is usually the sender's exact address, an unexpected request, or pressure to act fast — not typos.

items.myth: If an email comes from someone I know, it's safe.
items.fact: Attackers regularly spoof or hijack real accounts, including coworkers' — a familiar name doesn't confirm a message is genuine.
items.detail: If a request feels off, verify through a different channel, like a phone call, before acting on it.

items.fact: Phishing now happens over text, phone calls, QR codes, and chat apps like Teams — any channel that can carry a link or a request can carry an attempt.
items.detail: The pattern is always the same regardless of channel: urgency, a request, and pressure to act immediately.

items.myth: A password with a special character like "P@ssw0rd!" is strong.
items.fact: Length beats complexity — a longer plain phrase is harder to crack than a short password with symbol substitutions attackers already expect.
items.detail: "P@ssw0rd!" can be cracked in under a second; a random 16-character phrase can take centuries.

items.myth: You should change your password every 30-90 days.
items.fact: Frequent forced changes usually lead to weaker, more predictable passwords — a strong, unique password is fine to keep until there's a real reason to think it's been exposed.
items.detail: Most current guidance has moved away from mandatory rotation toward length, uniqueness, and watching for breaches.

items.myth: Reusing one strong password across a few accounts is fine, since it's strong.
items.fact: If any one of those accounts is breached, the same password immediately unlocks every other account using it — strength doesn't protect against reuse.
items.detail: A password manager makes using a different password per account realistic without memorizing them all.

items.myth: Social engineering is just a fancy word for lying.
items.fact: It's the deliberate use of urgency, authority, and trust to make you skip your normal checks — the manipulation is the point, not just the dishonesty.
items.detail: Attackers study how people react under pressure, then design a message specifically to trigger that reaction.

items.myth: Only careless or untrained people fall for social engineering.
items.fact: Well-designed social engineering is built to work on careful people too — it targets normal human responses to urgency and authority, not a lack of awareness.
items.detail: The goal of training isn't to make you suspicious of everything — it's to build a pause before acting on pressure.

items.myth: Reporting a mistake will get you in trouble.
items.fact: Reporting fast is what actually protects you and the company — the damage almost always comes from delay, not from the original click.
items.detail: Security teams would rather help with ten false alarms than find out about one real incident a week too late.

items.myth: If I'm not sure something is actually malicious, it's not worth reporting.
items.fact: Security teams would rather check a false alarm than miss a real one — uncertainty is exactly the reason to report, not a reason to stay quiet.
items.detail: A five-minute report is far cheaper than the hours it takes to contain an incident caught too late.
